items.explanation: Pitt won colonial cooperation by putting recruitment under colonial assemblies and promising London would reimburse their war expenses — respecting colonial sensitivities instead of commanding them.
options: A. Threatening reprisals by the British army
B. Threatening to leave colonists to fight France alone
C. Placing colonial troop recruitment in colonial hands
D. Paying colonial soldiers generous cash bonuses

items.explanation: Earlier parliamentary duties had been indirect taxes on trade. The Stamp Act was Parliament's first direct, internal tax on the colonists — paper, documents, dice — and it ignited the cry of 'no taxation without representation.'
options: A. It imposed massive new duties on colonial trade
B. It was Parliament's first-ever duty touching the colonies
C. It stripped revenue from colonial legislatures
D. It was Parliament's first direct tax on the colonists

items.explanation: In 1768 Adams denounced the Townshend duties as violations of the colonists' 'natural and constitutional rights,' making him the leading ideological voice of resistance in Massachusetts.
options: A. Benjamin Franklin
B. John Hancock
C. Samuel Adams
D. Patrick Henry
items.stem: Who called British taxes on the colonists 'infringements of their natural and constitutional rights'?

items.explanation: Far from shirking, the colonies raised nearly 24,000 men — almost as many as Britain's 25,000 regulars — so British complaints about colonial ingratitude rang hollow and bred mutual resentment.
options: A. The British resented how few colonists had aided the war effort
B. British soldiers were quartered in colonial homes
C. The British resented colonial trade with the French
D. Militiamen resented British officers' condescension

items.explanation: The 1774 Congress was still moderate: John Adams brokered a compromise firmly resisting taxation without consent while stopping short of the total boycott or military preparations that radicals wanted.
options: A. Demanded a total boycott of all British goods
B. Resolved to firmly resist taxation without their consent
C. Began seriously planning military action
D. Demanded Britain stop regulating colonial trade entirely

items.explanation: Dickinson's Letters from a Farmer warned that Parliament's taxes threatened colonial liberty and urged Americans to guard their rights jealously — the classic patriot argument short of independence.
options: A. Greater trust in the British government
B. Stronger central authority in London
C. Vigilant defense of American liberties
D. Immediate secession from the British Empire
items.stem: In the excerpt, what course is Dickinson urging on his fellow Americans?
items.stimulus:
Questions 6–8 refer to the following excerpt.

"A perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty, is absolutely requisite in all free states. The very texture of their constitution, in mixed government, demands it... Let us take care of our rights, and we therein take care of our prosperity."
—John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, 1767–1768 (abridged)

items.explanation: Dickinson wrote the Letters to oppose the Townshend Acts' new duties, arguing Parliament had no right to tax the colonies.
options: A. British strategy in the French and Indian War
B. New British taxes imposed on the colonies
C. The growth of royal absolutism in Britain
D. Religious divisions from the Great Awakening
